newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia seen returning to solid growth in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Colombia seen returning to solid growth in 1998.

text.p: Colombia should return to solid economic growth of about 5.3 percent in 1998, spurred by rising oil exports, an expected pickup in industrial output and a change in the central government, the head of a private economic think-tank said Wednesday.
"Real economic growth will be seen in 1998, with dynamism in all sectors," Mauricio Cardenas, director of the Fedesarrollo economic research group, told a capital markets seminar.

He said the economy was already in the process of a "slow recovery" from last year's sharp slowdown, but added that he saw gross domestic product growth of no more than about 3.8 percent in 1997 against government estimates of anywhere from 4.0 to 4.5 percent.
GDP growth last year was estimated in a recent, preliminary report from the National Planning Department at just 2.1 percent, a sharp decline from average growth of 4.5 percent over the past decade.
Cardenas said a buildup of inventories in 1996 would hurt industrial production this year.
But he predicted the manufacturing sector would rebound in 1998 along with most other parts of the economy.

He cited an expected surge in oil production as one factor supporting the return to bubbling growth rates. But Cardenas, differing from some other analysts, also said next year's presidential elections should be constructive for the economy.
"Election years are good in terms of economic performance because governments have historically used their last year to score political points by expanding the economy," he said.
